lines.text: One setting took 401(k) sign-ups from 37% to 86%.
lines.say: One setting took four oh one k sign-ups from thirty-seven to eighty-six percent.

lines.text: In a famous 2001 study, 37% of workers joined the 401(k) when they had to sign up. With automatic enrollment, 86% did.
lines.say: In a famous twenty oh one study, thirty-seven percent of workers joined the four oh one k when they had to sign up. With automatic enrollment, eighty-six percent did.

lines.text: Same company, same plan. The only thing that changed was the default.
lines.say: Same company, same plan. The only thing that changed was the default.

lines.text: That's the idea behind paying yourself first: savings leave on payday, before you get a chance to spend them.
lines.say: That's the idea behind paying yourself first. Savings leave on payday, before you get a chance to spend them.

lines.text: And it matters, because Americans saved just 4.1% of their disposable income in August 2026.
lines.say: And it matters, because Americans saved just four point one percent of their disposable income in August twenty twenty-six.

lines.text: Here's the math on a small automatic transfer: $100 every two weeks is $2,600 a year.
lines.say: Here's the math on a small automatic transfer. A hundred dollars every two weeks is twenty-six hundred dollars a year.

lines.text: Common ways people automate it: a split direct deposit, a payday transfer, a 401(k), or auto-increase.
lines.say: Common ways people automate it: a split direct deposit, a payday transfer, a four oh one k, or an automatic increase.

lines.text: Inertia usually works against saving. Automation flips it so doing nothing means saving.
lines.say: Inertia usually works against saving. Automation flips it, so doing nothing means you save.

lines.text: That's the money. Follow for more.
lines.say: That's the money. Follow for more.

post.ig:
One setting took 401(k) sign-ups from 37% to 86%.

Madrian & Shea (2001): 401(k) participation was 37% when workers had to opt in, 86% with automatic enrollment.
US personal saving rate: 4.1% of disposable income in August 2026 (BEA).
Example: $100 every two weeks = $2,600 a year.

Sources: Quarterly Journal of Economics (2001), BEA (Sept 30, 2026).
News and education, not financial advice.
